newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi marks anniversary of Buyoya's coup.
newsitem.headline: Burundi marks anniversary of Buyoya's coup.

text.p: Burundi's military leader Pierre Buyoya said on Friday he would fight for peace and unity, marking the first anniversary of a bloodless coup that brought him to power.

"I accept the challenge of implementing the peace process through negotiations and I appeal to all Burundians to support me in this project," he told 1,000 people at a stadium in Buyenzi, a suburb of the capital.

"My government has the power to restore the authority of the state, avoid the disintegration of Burundi's society, put an end to genocide and bring back security," Buyoya said on Thursday night in a nationwide address broadcast on state television.
Leaders of the pro-Hutu Frodebu party boycotted the rally as did Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, the ousted Hutu president who emerged in June after 10 months hiding in the U.S. embassy.
"Even if I received an invitation I would not go there as I cannot celebrate a coup d'etat," Ntibantunganya told Reuters.

Since seizing power, Buyoya, a retired major in the Tutsi-dominated army, has beefed up the army and pursued a policy of grouping mainly Hutu villagers in camps to prevent them giving support to rebels.

Regional states imposed sanctions shortly after the coup and demanded Buyoya open unconditional talks with rebel groups including the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), the main Hutu group fighting the army.
But the trade and transport sanctions were relaxed in April.

Buyoya said this week formal talks including CNDD would start next month in Arusha, north Tanzania. But talks with CNDD, which resulted in a pre-ceasefire agreement in April, have been fiercely criticised by fellow Tutsis.
Charles Mukasi, chairman of the pro-Tutsi Uprona party, said Buyoya's political record was a "lamentable failure."
More than 150,000 people have been killed in massacres and civil war in Burundi since the country's first freely-elected Hutu president was murdered in an attempted coup in October 1993.
Human rights groups have accused the army and rebels of massacring civilians. But army officers argue Buyoya's leadership has enabled them to take the war to the rebels.
"When it comes to the army, we now have the ways, means and size to fight. Before we didn't know who to trust," said Lieutenant-Colonel Longin Minani, a defence ministry adviser.

"Before the coup it was a two-headed government. They (Tutsis) couldn't suffer the thought that they were governed by Frodebu. Out of this disagreement came paralysis and out of that paralysis came anarchy...In that sense the coup brought a certain amount of order," an aid worker said.

Aid workers and the United Nations have protested Buyoya's regroupment policy, which has gathered an estimated 300,000 in camps. Another 350,000 are internally displaced out of a population of six million.
Buyoya first seized power in a coup in 1987 but lost democratic elections to Frodebu in 1993 and stepped down.
Analysts say that despite his efforts as a Tutsi moderate to further talks and bring peace, it will not be easy to heal the wounds of the bitter Hutu-Tutsi conflict in the tiny country.

"Even if many things have changed the most important thing, people's mentality, hasn't changed. People are still deeply divided," said Louis Marie Nindorera, director of the human rights group League Iteka.
